> **Working draft for instructor discussion · 2026-09-12.** The teaching sequence is flexible. Dates and weights below are a coordinated draft; outstanding instructor and administrative decisions are listed in the syllabus.

Nothing on this page is new. Every block below sat on the unit page the week you
built it, and you have been reading `for`, `if`, `def`, lists and indices since
Week 1 without being asked to type any of it.

Read end to end, the nine blocks describe the whole semester: a parameter set, a
sequence of operations, a solid assembled from its parts, a loop that places
things, a measurement that varies them, a surface divided into cells, data you did
not author, a shape written as a function, and that shape cut into parts a machine
can make.

The point is not that code is better than a graph. It is that they are the same
description. A node group and a function both take named inputs, do one thing, and
hand the result on. When you named an exposed input this semester you were writing
a signature; when you set a count you were bounding a loop; when you used Compare
and Switch you were writing an `if`.

**Optional, for extra credit.** Take one of your own definitions — not one of
these — and write it out as a working script, exposing the same named inputs you
exposed in the graph. It is worth up to five points on top of the final grade, it
is assessed on whether it runs and whether you can explain it, and nothing else in
the course depends on it.

### U02 — Transformations and CSG

```python
base  = box(6, 4, 3)
tower = box(2, 2, 6)
tower = move(tower, 2, 0, 3)

void  = cylinder(r=1, h=5)
void  = move(void, -1.5, 0, 0)

mass   = union(base, tower)
result = difference(mass, void)    # not difference(void, mass)
```

### U03 — Geometry from scratch

```python
verts = [[-w, -d, 0],              # 0
         [ w, -d, 0],              # 1
         [ w,  d, 0],              # 2
         [-w,  d, 0],              # 3
         [ 0,  0, h]]              # 4  apex

faces = [[0, 1, 4], [1, 2, 4],
         [2, 3, 4], [3, 0, 4],
         [0, 3, 2, 1]]             # the base — do not forget it

pyramid = mesh(verts, faces)
result  = difference(cube, pyramid)
```

### U04 — Arrays and lists

```python
points = []

for j in range(rows):                      # nested loop = grid
    offset = spacing / 2 if j % 2 else 0   # odd/even stagger
    for i in range(cols):
        z = amplitude * sin(i * frequency + phase)
        if 3 <= i <= 5:                    # Compare + Switch
            z = z + lift
        points.append([i * spacing + offset, j * row_gap, z])
```

### U05 — Attractors

```python
for p in points:
    d = distance(p, attractor)             # or min(...) over several
    t = (d - d_min) / (d_max - d_min)      # remap
    t = clamp(t, 0, 1)
    t = falloff(t)                         # linear, inverse, smooth, step
    size = out_min + t * (out_max - out_min)
    place(component, p, scale=size)
```

### U06 — Tessellation and lattices

```python
for cell in subdivide(surface, u, v):
    panel = morph(component, cell)         # component into the cell
    d = distance(center(cell), attractor)
    panel.aperture = remap(d, d_min, d_max, 0.1, 0.9)
    panel.depth    = remap(d, d_min, d_max, 2.0, 12.0)
    keep(panel)
```

### U07 — Point clouds and the transition to volumes

```python
cloud = load("site.ply")
print(len(cloud))                          # state this before

cloud = decimate(cloud, keep=0.05)
print(len(cloud))                          # and after

for p in cloud:
    p.density = len(within(cloud, p, radius))

volume = voxelize(cloud, size=0.5)
```

### U08 — Volumetric fields and signed distance

```python
def field(p):                              # a shape as a function
    a = sphere_sdf(p, center_a, r_a)
    b = box_sdf(p, center_b, size_b)
    return smooth_min(a, b, k)             # the blend comes free

grid    = sample(field, bounds, resolution)
surface = extract(grid, iso=0.0)           # where the field is zero
```

### U09 — Contour sections and physical parts

```python
sections = []
for k in range(count):
    z = z0 + k * interval
    sections.append(slice(volume, z))      # ordered, and order matters

for i, s in enumerate(sections):
    s = offset(s, kerf / 2)                # the blade has width
    label(s, i)
    nest(s, sheet)
```
